articles.title: Russians held at U.S. immigration detention center plan hunger strike over poor conditions
articles.body:
Russians held at U.S. immigration detention center plan hunger strike over poor conditions
Fourteen Russians held in an immigration detention center in the state of Georgia have signed a collective complaint about the conditions of their detention and announced that they plan to begin a hunger strike. Copies of the complaint were obtained by Vot Tak, Agentstvo, and The Insider. Four sources familiar with the conditions in detention confirmed the document’s authenticity to Agentstvo. Here’s what we know so far.
Russians held in an immigration jail in Georgia say they are not treated for illness, are fed poorly, and have limited contact with the outside world
One of the most serious allegations in the collective complaint is the lack of medical care. The Russians say that while detained, they receive almost no treatment. Emergency care is only provided in cases of loss of consciousness or severe bleeding. For fever, high blood pressure, or acute pain, detainees may have to wait “a week or more” for treatment.
Alexei Kovalko, one of the authors of the complaint, said he once lost consciousness while having blood drawn. After he was revived, he asked staff to let him lie down, still feeling weak and dizzy. He was taken to a room that contained only a toilet and left lying on the bare concrete floor for several hours.
Kovalko said an even more acute problem is dental care. “My personal experience: numerous complaints about tooth pain and requests to see a dentist have been ignored for almost two years. They aren’t even registered in the system,” the Russian wrote in the complaint.
He and the other authors of the complaint also cite poor-quality water and bad food (they are mostly given canned and frozen food); cold cells (they have to sleep in their clothes); and noise in common areas (televisions there aren’t turned off until 2 a.m., which interferes with sleep, especially since earplugs are banned).
The complaint separately lists problems with communication: paper mail is delivered selectively, email is unavailable, and phone calls are expensive. Many of the people held at the jail are going through court proceedings over their immigration status, and these rules severely limit their ability to communicate with lawyers and defend themselves.
“The goal of this facility is to deport the maximum number of people and create conditions in which it’s impossible to defend your case in immigration court,” the complaint states. Its authors believe this is confirmed by the behavior of the detention center’s warden. He has repeatedly told the people held there that they will not be living in the U.S., and once told the Russians: “Don’t worry, we’ll send you back to your cozy Gulag.”
The immigration jail in Georgia was converted from a regular prison. Conditions there have largely remained the same
The immigration detention center named in the collective complaint is the D. Ray James Correctional Facility in Folkston, Georgia, named after a former mayor of the city. It is owned by GEO Group, one of the two largest private prison operators in the U.S.
The facility previously operated as a federal prison. In 2025, it was converted into an immigrant detention center. The people held there are not necessarily criminals and are not serving criminal sentences; for them, detention means being deprived of their liberty over a possible deportation while their case is being considered in immigration court. In practice, however, conditions in detention centers can resemble those in prisons.
Dmitry Valuev, president of the organization Russian America for Democracy in Russia (RADR), told Vot Tak that conditions in American immigration detention centers are difficult, but not everywhere are they as harsh as at the D. Ray James facility in Folkston.
“There are select detention centers where vegetables and fresh fruit are given out regularly, even daily, but there are many others where fruits and vegetables aren’t part of the regular diet. The same goes for medical services — people with chronic illnesses suffer a great deal, because treatment in detention centers is mostly very basic, without advanced diagnostics,” Valuev said.
He stressed that immigration detention centers are normally meant for short-term detention — up to several weeks — and that food and medical care standards there are designed with that in mind. In practice, however, people can remain in detention for years, and in those cases, the conditions effectively become torturous.
Russians (and detainees from other countries) plan to start a hunger strike. They want to be transferred to another facility
The collective complaint bears the signatures of 14 people. According to materials obtained by outlets that received a copy of the complaint, all of them are Russian. Among them are the complaint’s authors, Alexei Kovalko and Alexander Borovkov, and 12 other men who have been held in Folkston for five to 30 months. Kovalko, for example, has been in the jail for more than two years — 28 months.
The Russians relayed through relatives that they plan to declare a hunger strike on October 6 to protest the conditions of their detention. According to them, about 50 detainees in total plan to take part in the hunger strike — not only Russians but also Latin Americans, Iranians, Afghans, Chinese nationals, and people from other countries.
“Everyone wants to be released or transferred to other detention centers where they could get a fair hearing on their cases, bail requests, and petitions. At the same time, they’re demanding improved detention conditions,” Polina Gerdyukova, the wife of Andrei Gerdyukov — one of the signatories of the complaint who has been held in detention since February 2026 — told the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo.
The flow of Russians seeking asylum in the U.S. increased after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. People who end up in immigration jails are usually those who crossed the border from Mexico and requested asylum in the U.S., or who were detained later while already in the country. As of spring 2026, RADR estimated the number of Russians in U.S. detention centers at 700–800 people.
After Donald Trump returned to power, U.S. authorities began detaining and deporting foreigners more aggressively. RADR believes that around 300–400 Russians may have been deported over the past year alone. They are being sent back to Russia even though they may face criminal charges or military conscription there.
At least two cases are known in which Russians who had sought asylum in the U.S. were detained on criminal charges after being deported back to Russia. The first involves serviceman Artem Vovchenko: after arriving in Russia, he was sent to a pretrial detention center on charges of abandoning his military unit, but he managed to get transferred to a civilian hospital and escaped from there. The second case is the prosecution of businessman and activist Leonid Melekhin, who was ultimately sentenced to six years on charges of justifying terrorism.

articles.title: Commandos land from German submarine on Scottish coast
articles.body:
British commandos have come ashore at Cape Wrath from a German attack submarine and directed the guns of a Portuguese frigate onto targets inland, during the largest test of every part of the UK Commando Force in fifteen years, according to the Royal Navy.
The landing took place during Exercise Strike Warrior, which the service describes as the first occasion since the war in Afghanistan on which all the specialist elements of the formation have worked together. More than 2,000 personnel from six nations are taking part, drawn from the United Kingdom, the Netherlands, Canada, Germany, Norway and the United States, and deployed across the Western Isles, the North-West Approaches, Galloway, the Borders and the North Sea.
Navy and Army commandos from 148 Battery Commando Forward Observation Battery, the unit trained to carry out reconnaissance and call down naval gunfire from behind enemy lines, left the submarine in inflatable raiding boats and established an observation post on the cliffs at the most north-westerly point of mainland Britain. From there they directed the guns of the Portuguese warship NRP Dom Francisco de Almeida onto positions ashore.
The battery’s operations officer, who cannot be named for operational reasons, said: “This level of complexity and coordination of live assets has not been achieved by 148 Battery for nearly 30 years.
“We wanted to demonstrate to our partners across the United Kingdom Commando Force, wider UK Defence and NATO Special Operations Force community the type of missions we are prepared to execute against future threats.
“Warfighting is our focus, and we are prepared to employ specialist assets to deliver Multi-Domain Fires and Targeting.”
Three navies were involved in the single sequence at Cape Wrath. The German submarine found the targets, the commandos put themselves ashore without being seen, and the Portuguese ship supplied the firepower. The Royal Navy has not identified the submarine.
Earlier in the exercise the same battery controlled the naval gunfire of ships from Standing NATO Maritime Group One, the alliance’s standing task group in northern European waters. The Dutch frigate HNLMS Van Amstel and the Royal Canadian Navy frigate HMCS St John’s both worked with commandos in observation posts to bring their guns onto targets.
Eight warships and 19 aircraft are taking part in Strike Warrior, which began on 28 September and finishes on Friday. Alongside the gunnery serials, the exercise has covered amphibious landings, boarding operations, intelligence and surveillance missions, logistics and sustainment, maritime security and anti-submarine warfare. Commandos have flown drone missions including strikes and resupply to troops in contact, and have built underground medical facilities.
Cape Wrath matters to this kind of training because it is the only place in Britain, and one of very few in Europe, where warships can fire live rounds at a land target. The range takes in Garvie Island off the headland, and the combination of the cliffs behind and the open Atlantic in front is what allows observation parties to work close to live naval gunfire.
The participation of a German boat and a Portuguese frigate alongside Dutch and Canadian ships reflects how the Commando Force now expects to operate, which is as the land element of a NATO maritime group rather than as a national force working alone. Norway and the United States also have personnel committed, and the stated purpose of the exercise is rehearsing allied crisis response in the High North and the North Atlantic.

articles.title: Ukrainian drones kill two in Moscow Region – officials
articles.body:
Ukrainian drones kill two in Moscow Region – officials
Two civilians have been killed and nine injured after Ukraine launched 650 drones toward Moscow and the surrounding region overnight, local officials have said.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said in the early hours of Tuesday that most of the UAVs were destroyed at “distant lines,” while 134 were intercepted on the approaches to Moscow itself.
In Moscow Region, air defenses neutralized 185 drones, Governor Andrey Vorobyov reported. A 20-year-old man was killed in the settlement of Radumlya, northwest of Moscow, while rescuers found a 71-year-old man dead beneath the rubble of a destroyed private home in Barybino, south of the capital, with a woman in the same building receiving injuries.
A man in Pokrovskoye, west of Moscow, was hospitalized with shrapnel wounds, while two residents of the Istra area, also west of the capital, were taken to hospital. Three people in Lyakhovo, south of Moscow, received medical care but declined hospitalization, Vorobyov added.
Vorobyov said a total of 47 private homes were damaged across the region. In Lobanovo, south of the capital, windows and balcony glazing were blown out in four apartments, while a nearby boiler house was also damaged. Three cars were hit, and a small fire at a warehouse in Litvinovo, northwest of Moscow, was extinguished, according to the governor.
According to the Russian Defense Ministry, a total of 868 Ukrainian drones were intercepted across the country overnight.
On Tuesday, Rodion Miroshnik, the head of the Russian Foreign Ministry mission tracking alleged Ukrainian war crimes, told TASS that 29 civilians, including two children, were killed and 206 injured in Ukrainian attacks on Russian regions over the past week alone. He added that 98% were victims of drone strikes.
Ukraine has ramped up attacks deep into Russia in recent weeks, targeting oil refineries and civilian infrastructure. After Vladimir Zelensky pledged to escalate the strikes even further, the Russian Defense Ministry said on Sunday that it had “taken note” of the statement, vowing to intensify attacks on Ukrainian military and defense industrial facilities as well as related infrastructure. Moscow maintains it never targets civilians.

Russia Says Ukraine Just Launched Its Biggest Strike of the War—1,750 Drones and 17 Flamingo Missiles
Ukraine launched what Russia described as the largest combined drone and missile strike of the war, with 1,750 fixed-wing UAVs and 17 Flamingo cruise missiles allegedly used against targets across Russia over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed on October 6.
Moscow also said its air defenses intercepted two guided aerial bombs and one HIMARS rocket during the same period. The figures have not been independently verified.

If accurate, the drone count would exceed Ukraine’s previous reported record from August 18, when Russian authorities said 1,671 UAVs were detected over 15 regions, occupied Crimea, and the Black and Azov seas.
The reported use of 17 Flamingo cruise missiles would also represent a major jump from earlier strikes, when launches were generally reported in groups of three to six.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said 11 regions, occupied Crimea, and targets over the Azov Sea came under attack overnight.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said 650 drones were flying toward the Russian capital during the attack. He initially reported 105 intercepted on approach to Moscow and later said another 68 had been destroyed.
Moscow region Governor Andrei Vorobyov said 185 UAVs were intercepted across 16 municipalities.
Russian authorities also reported damage to 47 private homes in Volokolamsk, Stupino, Dmitrov, Naro-Fominsk, Serpukhov, Domodedovo and Istra, as well as damage to an apartment building in the village of Lobanovo.
The scale of the overnight attack also caused major disruption at Moscow’s airports, where more than 200 flights were delayed or canceled after midnight.
Sheremetyevo saw the largest impact, with about 47 departing flights and 106 arrivals affected. Another 28 departures and 23 arrivals were disrupted at Vnukovo, while Domodedovo reported changes to four flights.

articles.title: Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
articles.body:

Putin’s Family War Games Are Now in Full Swing
What began as a Kremlin-backed “patriotic” family initiative has grown into nationwide military-style competitions where children as young as 11 train alongside their parents, handle weapons, practice battlefield skills, and are coached by veterans of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Russia has expanded its military-style youth training into entire households, bringing parents and children together for nationwide war games that include shooting, grenade throwing, drone operations, and tactical exercises.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to The Barents Observer on October 6, families from nearly every Russian region are taking part in the “Family Zarnitsa” competition, a Kremlin-backed initiative promoted as a way to strengthen “traditional values” and ties between generations.
Teams consist of two adults and two children aged 11 or older. Participants wear military-style uniforms and compete in exercises including grenade throwing, dismantling and reassembling Kalashnikov assault rifles, marksmanship, tactical field operations, first aid, and evacuating simulated casualties.
The training grounds are designed to resemble combat environments, while each family is assigned a coach who is a veteran of Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The project was formally presented in early 2025 by Russian Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilova and was later backed by Vladimir Putin.
“Today, the ‘Family Zarnitsa’ project brings families together, strengthens the bond between generations, and integrates veterans of the Special Military Operation into a system of mentoring and patriotic education for young people,” Tsivilova said, using Russia’s official term for its war against Ukraine.
The competition is organized by several Kremlin-linked groups involved in the militarization of Russian youth, including Yunarmiya, VOIN, and Movement of the First, alongside the state-run Defenders of the Fatherland fund.
Russia has spent years expanding military and patriotic education among children and teenagers through organizations such as Yunarmiya and VOIN, whose combined membership now reaches hundreds of thousands of young Russians.
After regional qualification rounds, successful families advance to a national final. One of this year’s participants was the Maksimenko family from Zaozersk, a closed naval town on Russia’s Kola Peninsula.
The family defeated teams from Pechenga, Lovozero, and Murmansk before reaching the national final in Volgograd, where it finished 10th among 89 teams.
Yevgeniya Maksimenko, the family’s mother, said the competition included drones, mines, shooting, grenades, radio communications, and first aid, but described teamwork as its main lesson.
“We’ve become a REAL team. There are no ‘mums,’ ‘dads,’ or ‘kids’ here,” she wrote on social media.
Maksimenko has also been active in Russia’s ruling United Russia party. In 2025, she received an award from former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev for her work with the party’s women’s movement. Her eldest daughter, Liza, is a member of the VOIN military youth organization in Murmansk.
Earlier, in March 2025, Putin ordered the nationwide launch of “Family Zarnitsa,” a military-patriotic competition for parents and children proposed by Deputy Defense Minister Anna Tsivilyova. The initiative was designed to combine physical challenges with patriotic education and activities focused on Russian history and culture.

articles.body:

Ukraine Records 11,000+ Deep Strikes in September, Hits More Russian Air Defenses Than Ever
Ukrainian forces recorded more than 11,000 confirmed strikes against Russian targets located over 20 kilometers (12 miles) from the front line in September, while also hitting a record number of Russian air defense systems, Ukraine’s Ministry of Defense reported on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the ministry, September marked the first time the number of confirmed strikes beyond 20 kilometers exceeded 11,000 in a single month. Ukrainian forces also recorded their highest number of strikes against targets located more than 50 kilometers (31 miles) from the front.
The largest concentration of these longer-range strikes occurred along the Russian military logistics route linking temporarily occupied Mariupol with Crimea, the ministry said.
September also saw the highest number of Russian air defense assets hit since the launch of Ukraine’s ePoints battlefield performance program. The targets included radar systems, with one Russian air defense asset struck at a distance of 552 kilometers (343 miles).
In total, Ukrainian units recorded 33,087 confirmed strikes against Russian personnel during September. Only March and April saw higher monthly figures in 2026 under the ePoints program.
The Defense Ministry said all results counted by the program are supported by video recorded in Ukraine’s DELTA battlefield management system and subsequently verified by the Brave1 defense innovation cluster.
Ukraine also reported increased effectiveness against Russian Shahed-type attack drones. Ukrainian forces downed 28% more Shahed-type UAVs in September than in August, despite Russia changing its aerial attack tactics and deploying a growing number of jet-powered drones.
The ePoints program tracks battlefield results across Ukrainian military units, allowing defense officials to compare the effectiveness of different weapons and tactics and expand successful approaches across the Defense Forces.
Earlier, Ukraine’s Unmanned Systems Forces reported hitting or destroying 300 Russian air defense assets in the first 261 days of 2026, including 162 air defense systems, 124 radar complexes, and 14 electronic warfare systems.

articles.title: Live Q&A: Will an unpopular Iran war cost Trump the midterms? Our reporters answer your questions
articles.body:
Will the Iran war cost Trump in the US midterm elections? Your questions answered
The war with Iran is reshaping America ahead of the midterms – how will it affect US voters at the polls? Guardian political and foreign correspondents answered your questions
Thanks everyone for participating in our live conversation ahead of the 3 November US midterm elections. We’ll be back with more conversations throughout the month of October, providing context on a range of important topics as you head to the polls.
Will Trump be held to account on claims of corruption?
Mikeyboyuser asked: Do you think that Trump will ever be held to account for his rampant corruption. Can he ever be prosecuted for his blatant abuse of the constitution in regards to “personal gain while in office”.
Lastly, I have heard it muted that he may well advance his daughter in law as a presidential candidate. Could this be illegal, given Trump’s disregard for the law would the GOP be held culpable should it happen. Thanks.
Robert: I have written on the possible political and electoral consequences of Trump’s corruption today. You can read it here.
The question of Trump’s presidential prosecution for malfeasance may have been rendered moot by the 2024 Supreme Court ruling giving him broad immunity for acts committed while in office. Trump has also attempted to take further steps to protect himself in future in the future of a Department of Justice-driven settlement that would have barred the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) from investigating his tax affairs, or those of his family. The settlement was later struck down by a judge. So that may provide an avenue for future probes.
Would Republican losses in the midterms actually limit Trump’s power?
idlehanz asks: Given Trump’s proclivity for riding roughshod over almost anything, is it a certainty that losses in the midterms would actually limit his ability to cause more chaos?
Lauren: Predicting what Trump might do is never easy! But I would expect he will continue to push the limits of his executive authority if he can’t get his legislative priorities through the Congress. That would set up even more legal clashes between the branches. We could also see him veto Democratic-led legislation or possibly hold up or refuse to sign must-pass bills as a way to extract from Congressional Democrats. He could, as many presidents do later in their term, look abroad and try to further push his foreign policy agenda.
What is the future of the Republican party without Trump?
TeeDubyaBee asks: Once Trump has shuffled off this mortal coil, is the fate of the Republicans likely to be that of the Tory party’s slide into irrelevance over here in the UK or are political identities more nailed-on in the U.S., regardless of the leader?
Robert: The Republican party is unlikely to disappear from the American political scene. A more probable outcome is that it will evolve and shape-shift after the Trump era, to adapt itself to whatever the prevalent future mood is. In the US, the two-party system is a fixed reality in a sense that is not the case for any European democracy, including Britain, even though it - like the US - uses a first-past-the-post electoral system. Both the Republicans and the Democrats have known many guises down the generations; evidenced by the historical reality that the Republicans were the party of Abraham Lincoln and forged in an existential struggle against slavery, an institution defended by the Democrats of the day. Later generations of southern Democrats staunchly upheld segregation, until the civil rights legislation of the 1960s triggered a party realignment that has more or less survived to the present day. In summary, America’s two-party system seems fixed in stone, but it is mutable. The character of parties evolve for the sake of electoral survival and this is likely to be the future fate of the Republicans.
Will there be accountability for the Minab school bombing?
Ponteland_Paul asks: At what point will those responsible for the Shajarah Tayyebeh elementary school attack killing 175 people be held accountable? If at all?
Robert: This is an excellent and heart-rending question to which there may be no satisfactory answer. The attack on the school in the southern Iranian city of Minab took place in the very first day of the war and went far beyond any standard war narrative explanations of “collateral damage.” Most of those killed were school girls. To this day, the US had not taken responsibility for the strike, although multiple independent investigations - including by the United Nations and Amnesty International - have concluded that it was caused by an American strike. All the indications are that it was a genuine blunder, perhaps caused by flawed or out-of-date intelligence. None of this will appease Iran, where memories are still vivid of the 1988 shooting down of a civilian passenger plane flying over the Gulf by an American war ship, the USS Vincennes. On that occasion, all 290 people on board were killed, including 66 children. The US later expressed regret for the incident, citing misidentification of the plane, and paid compensation to the victims’ families. However, the captain of the Vincennes, Captain William C. Rogers, was not subject to any disciplinary procedures and later received a Legion of Merit award. The seems to bode ill for any kind of accountability process being enacted over the school strike. Coincidentally, the Trump administration is aggressively targeting the International Criminal Court, imposing sanctions and financial restrictions on its officials and judges, after it issued arrest warrants against Israeli leaders over their actions in Gaza. It is possible to interpret that action as a warning shot to any international body contemplating trying to get accountability and justice in Minab.
KafkasDog asks: As it’s increasingly clear that Trump is not mentally fit, and that allowing him to continue in his role further may (likely?) decimate the economy, if the Dems can secure, say, 60+ seats in the Senate, should they pursue Article 25?
Lauren: A 60-plus majority! Sure things are looking good for Democrats, but not that good. But as I’m based in Los Angeles, a city Trump just last night joked he might “let them take out” - I will indulge the question. There are many Democrats who have long believed (since Trump 1.0) that he was not fit to serve. But then like now the process for actually involuntarily invoking the 25th Amendment originates with the vice president and the cabinet, not Congress. That alone should tell you how likely it is. Even then, if it were to reach Congress, which it would only if there was a dispute between the president and his vice president and cabinet over his capacity to serve, Congress would need a two-thirds majority in both chambers to install the vice president over the president.
I think the question Democrats are more likely to confront is whether they should again pursue impeachment against the president. And on that question, the party is really divided. While many believe he has committed impeachable offenses, they also recognize that their standing remains low and voters want action on the issues they care most about - the economy. Given that there is almost no likelihood of a Senate majority great enough to convict the president, I think Democrats feel this avenue is likely less fruitful than using their political capital to push through legislation that they hope will repair their standing, give them some credibility ahead of 2028, and ideally for them, knee-cap Trump’s movement that way.
Richard Ulmer in Tampa, Florida asks in a reader callout: Why doesn’t Congress stop a war that they didn’t approve of?
Robert: Simple question, to which there is no simple answer. Congress does have the power to impede or limit a war for which it has not voted. But the particular trajectory of the Iran conflict combined with Trump’s powerful grip on a Republican-controlled legislature has given him added flexibility. The 1973 War Powers Resolution - originally passed in the wake of the Vietnam war and intended to rein in a so-called “imperial president” - lays down that the administration must inform congress within 48 of committing forces to military action and must withdraw the forces within 60 to 90 days unless Congress votes to authorize the war or extend the time frame. Trump has been able to circumvent these restrictions through legal sleight of hand. For example, the original conflict was suspended in early April - before the 60-day period had been reached - by a de facto ceasefire that was later formalized through the signing of a memorandum of understanding between Iran and US. When that agreement subsequently collapsed, the White House argued that the 60-day threshold started again from scratch. More generally, Trump has invoked his constitutional powers under Article II, Section 2 of the constitution, which asserts that the president is empowered to order targeted strikes, defend US forces abroad, or respond to threats abroad without congressional authorization. Trump has also been able to reframe his actions as “defensive” by switching the primary goal of the war to re-opening the strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway that is a conduit for one-fifth of the world’s oil. Iran’s closure of it in response to being attacked has presented a major challenge to the US and global economy. In short, the Congress did not approve the war, and while its constitutional and legislative powers give it the ability to challenge and hamper Trump’s actions, the power inherent in the presidency does not invest it with the powers to stop it per se.
Elizabeth Knudson, a student journalist at American University, also asks: Mike Rogers [GOP candidate for US Senate in Michigan] and Ashley Hinson [GOP Iowa Congresswoman] have been rather vocal about their dissent toward Trump due to the war. Why them specifically? Are their states’ constituencies most impacted by the war? Are there any other senate candidates who may also feel hostility toward Trump for the war, due to the war impacting their state worse than others?
Lauren: Both are in incredibly tight races. The war is unpopular and they don’t want to be seen as cheerleaders for a war that the voters they hope to represent are opposed to. Particularly in Iowa, where Hinson is running for Senate, the war is driving up the costs of essential operating inputs like diesel and fertilizer. This comes atop Trump’s trade war, which had already squeezed US farmers.
In both states, the Democratic candidates are pounding them on affordability and cost-of-living and being publicly supportive of the war can dilute the Republicans’ ability to respond.
Will the Iran war split the Republican party irreparably?
Elizabeth Knudson, Washington DC, student journalist at American University asks in a callout question: For a class project my group and I are covering the impacts of the Iran war on the Republican party. We want to know how the war is dividing the party on the inside and also swaying support for Trump on the outside.
Is the war likely to split the Republican party irreparably? If yes, what might that mean for future elections?
Lauren: That’s great! What an interesting topic. I think the midterms will be the first test, but like your question hints at, the impact could be long-lasting.
It’s too hard to say if it has split the party irreparably, but it has certainly fractured Trump’s MAGA movement. Trump promised no new “forever wars,” and from our reporting in 2024 and since, we know that many supporters believed him. It’s a powerful promise, and for many voters, he clearly broke it. At the same time, there are still neo-conservatives and foreign policy hawks in the Republican party who support the war, in theory, even if there are signs many Republicans are losing faith in the administration’s ability to wage it successfully. As for what it means for future elections, I think the war and its legacy will follow Trump administration officials who may be considering higher office in 2028 – think JD Vance or Marco Rubio. It could also be another reason for voters already extremely disillusioned with American politics and the two-party system to disengage. We know Trump won a lot of voters who were angry with the status-quo and wanted something different. And for them, if he couldn’t deliver on a core promise - and many voters did see keeping the US out of foreign wars as a key part of his platform - then they may feel like there’s no point in voting.
If Republicans lose control of both houses, do Democrats have a plan for what's next?
paxmansbeard asks: Should the Republicans lose control of both houses, do the Democrats have a plan for what happens next? It could work against them in the long run if they don’t have anything apart from not being fascist..
Lauren: This is, to me, the million dollar question. (Is million too small these days, billion-dollar?) My colleagues and I have documented the bubbling anger – not just at Trump but at the entire political system and establishment of both parties. This cycle we’ve really seen this flare on the left, where insurgent candidates toppled several long-serving incumbents on a message of ideological and generational change.
But to your question, Democrats have been struggling to define themselves and rally around an agenda that isn’t “anti-Trump” since his first term. What they decide to prioritize - even if they don’t have a filibuster - or veto - proof majorities will set the stage for the 2028 presidential campaign and beyond. If we take them at their word, I’d guess their priority will be on legislation focused on reducing costs, think housing, groceries, childcare, and eldercare. I also expect they would want to renew the now-expired ACA tax credits and push to restore or address cuts made to Medicaid.
Has the war created a gap between Trump’s promises on affordability vs. the reality?
Eddie from Minnesota, USA, asks in a callout question: Has the war in Iran finally created a gap between this administration’s false promises and the reality of how unaffordable living in the U.S. has become?
Joseph Gedeon: Right, I don’t think the war created the gap so much as it made it impossible to ignore. Affordability has been the issue in American politics for about a decade…think about Bernie running in 2016 and 2020 with healthcare, student debt and wages. In the last election, Trump was running squarely on prices and inflation. Mamdani won in New York last year on rent freezes, affordability, free buses, etc, months before any of this. People knew that life was expensive pre-war.
Trump spent the 2024 campaign saying he’d bring prices down, including a pledge to slash energy costs, and he’s spent a lot of his time back in office insisting things are going great and that worrying about pesky affordability is overblown (anyone else remember when he was coming at the Biden administration from the other side???). One obvious wrinkle is January of this year, when the EIA was forecasting gas prices to fall this year, then he kicks off his surprise war alongside Israel, and inflation has instead gone from 2.4% that month to 3.4% by July. Vance himself said keeping oil and gas cheap was “goal number one”. As you know, the war is the opposite of cheap: it has cost $45.1 billion so far, and that’s not the full bill. It doesn’t include repairs to damaged bases and buildings — and the CBO estimates it could keep costing another $2-3 billion a month. The CBO also says the war will keep inflation about half a point higher than it otherwise would have been into early 2027.
Democrats might win in November - does that change anything?
NorthLondonIsRed asks: Since Congress’s war powers resolution against Trump’s Iran war was purely symbolic, how much real leverage would a Democratic-controlled Congress actually have to rein in the war after the midterms – or is this more about punishing Trump electorally than changing policy?
Robert Tait: A Democrat-controlled Congress could actually hold substantial powers to impede, hinder and scrutinize the White House’s conduct of the war. There is little doubt that the Iran leadership is aware of this and, consequently, have been prepared to keep fighting at least until a new Congress is sworn in. Congress’s most immediate impact could be its power of the purse. It is Congress that holds constitutional authority to appropriate funds for military operations. In practical terms, it could attach language to defense appropriations forbidding the use of congressionally-mandated funds for kinetic action against Iran without prior congressional authorization. It could withhold funds or refuse to grant supplemental war appropriations. Such moves could starve the operation of funds over time. It would not necessarily halt hostilities immediately. Trump has shown willingness to override Congress and break democratic norms, and he is likely, in the short term, to raid other budgetary areas to get the funds. But Congress’s actions would be more than symbolic. Besides budgetary considerations, it also has the power to stage hearings holding Pentagon and intelligence officials accountable under oath for their decisions, a spectacle that has the potential to put the war’s unpopularity at the forefront of public consciousness.
Will Democrats regaining control of congress be enough to end the war?
Roxanne Magnuson from Oregon, USA asks in a reader callout: Even if Democrats are successful in regaining the congressional balance, will that be enough influence to end this war? How can it be accomplished?
Lauren Gambino: Not necessarily. Trump has said he thinks Iran is waiting for the midterm elections to reach a deal, hoping that Republican losses will give Tehran an edge in negotiations. If he’s right, the post-election period could see efforts to reach a lasting deal even before a new Congress is sworn in in January. But if that doesn’t happen, and assuming Democrats win at least one chamber of Congress, they could use their new powers to launch public hearings, subpoena defense officials and generally demand more transparency regarding the war’s objectives and costs - both in terms of lives and taxpayer dollars. For example, my colleague Joseph has written extensively about Democrats’ demands for more information about the treatment of servicemembers wounded in the war, as well as the decision-making that led to a 28 February strike on a school in Minab, Iran, which killed more than 150 civilians, most of them children.
Democrats have promised to continue to introduce war powers resolutions as a symbol of the growing bipartisan discontent with the conflict, though Trump would retain the ultimate veto power.
Democrats could also leverage Congress’s “power of the purse” to try to reign Trump in through the budget process - ie “defunding” the war. The Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan Congressional scorekeeper, estimates the war will cost a minimum of $2bn a month - so, in theory, the next time the White House asks for additional money to fund the war, Democrats could say no.
Welcome to our latest US midterms live Q&A – just over a month away from election day on 3 November.
The war with Iran has had major implications for Americans’ wallets, government spending and US foreign policy. It’s has also been an important factor in reshaping the political landscape as the war enters its eighth month, with the 2026 US midterms quickly approaching.
Our team of reporters has helped readers understand the costs of the war and political consequences for Trump and candidates running in November. So, how could the war affect US voters at the polls?
Joining us on Tuesday at 12pm ET are senior political correspondent Lauren Gambino, political breaking news reporter Joseph Gedeon, global affairs correspondent Andrew Roth, data editor Will Craft and political correspondent Robert Tait.

articles.title: French armed forces test-fire new nuclear-capable missile — news agency
articles.body:
PARIS, October 6. /TASS/. The French Armed Forces have test-fired a new nuclear missile, the AFP news agency reported.
The missile without a warhead was launched from a submarine, it said, citing the Elysee Palace and the Ministry of Defense.
The agency noted that French President Emmanuel Macron observed the test firing from aboard a French Navy frigate.
According to AFP, the missile, the third version of the M51 strategic sea-launched ballistic missile, which entered service a year ago, did not carry a nuclear warhead and landed "in the North Atlantic, hundreds of kilometers from any coastline," the ministry specified.

articles.title: Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones Now Make Up 40% of Attacks on Ukraine—But Could Rise to 80%
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia’s Jet-Powered Drones Now Make Up 40% of Attacks on Ukraine—But Could Rise to 80%
Russia is increasingly using jet-powered drones in attacks against Ukraine, RBC-Ukraine reported, citing Deputy Air Force Commander Yurii Cherevashenko. Such systems now account for approximately 40% of all UAVs deployed in strikes, with their share potentially rising to around 80% in the future.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Speaking during a meeting of a temporary investigative commission, Cherevashenko said Russia had stepped up its use of jet-powered drones beginning in July. On some operational directions, such UAVs already account for up to 60% of Russian drone strikes.
“And the figure continues to grow. We predict that around 80% of drones used in strikes will be jet-powered,” Cherevashenko said.
According to the Air Force official, the share of jet-powered drones in Russian attacks is expected to continue rising and could eventually reach approximately 80%.
As Russia expands its use of jet-powered drones, Ukraine is developing new systems to counter them. Several types of small anti-aircraft missiles are being prepared for operational deployment, with the first results expected in the second half of October.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced the development during a joint press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on October 4. He said the new interceptors had not yet been used operationally but were expected to be deployed later this month.
“There are several types of them. We will obviously see the results this month. Toward the end, in the second half of this month, we expect to see the results. You asked about their use and how widespread it is. So far, there has been no such use. It is yet to happen,” Zelenskyy said in response to a journalist’s question.
Ukraine is also working on five high-speed interceptor drone models intended to counter jet-powered attack UAVs. Zelenskyy said that one of the five models had advanced far enough for production to potentially reach around 400 units by the end of October.
The remaining four interceptor models are still undergoing testing.

articles.title: India expands Navy’s BrahMos strike capability
articles.body:
India expands Navy’s BrahMos strike capability
India has contracted for more BrahMos missile launchers and fire-control systems for its Navy warships, expanding deployment of its primary maritime-strike weapon across the fleet.
The Defense Ministry signed the roughly $69 million contract with BrahMos Aerospace Private Limited in New Delhi on Tuesday. The order covers fire-control systems and launchers for Indian Navy ships and was made under a scheme to buy items that are indigenously designed and manufactured.
Several frontline Indian warships including destroyers and frigates already are armed with BrahMos missiles. New ships commissioned in recent years have received the system as standard equipment, while older vessels are being retrofitted in phases as part of a wider push to expand BrahMos deployment across the fleet by 2030, reports said.
BrahMos can be launched vertically or at an incline from naval platforms and is capable of striking both ships and land targets at extended ranges at supersonic speed.
The Indian Navy has operated BrahMos since 2005, when its anti-ship variant was integrated onto Rajput-class destroyers. The system has since become the service’s principal surface-to-surface weapon.
The latest purchase follows much larger contracts signed in 2024 when the missiles were ordered for the Navy’s combat and training requirements, along with additional shipborne BrahMos systems.
BrahMos Aerospace is a joint venture between India’s Defense Research and Development Organization and Russia’s NPO Mashinostroyenia. The program has produced ship-, land-, and air-launched versions of the supersonic cruise missile.
The new project will have at least 68% indigenous content and involve Indian companies, including micro, small, and medium enterprises. The ministry said the program is expected to generate employment over three years while increasing domestic participation in advanced military technology.

articles.title: Seoul backs Ukraine, but sanctioned tankers carried fuel from South Korea to Russia
articles.body:
Seven tankers made 14 trips from South Korea to Russia's Far East in July and August, carrying more than 176,000 metric tons of fuel, most of it diesel, the Guardian found in a 6 October analysis of port records and ship-tracking data. The UK and EU have sanctioned three of the ships, and one loaded its fuel from another tanker at sea off South Korea instead of at a terminal.
Ukrainian strikes have cut Russia's fuel output as Moscow scrambles for supplies, while fuel loaded at South Korean ports has flowed to Russia. Loadings began to surge in July, the same month South Korean President Lee Jae-myung pledged $100 million for Ukraine's reconstruction, the Guardian reported. That creates a tension in Seoul's policy toward the war: South Korea has provided Ukraine with humanitarian and non-lethal aid but ruled out sending weapons directly, while the fuel trade appears legal under South Korean law even though three of the tankers are under UK and EU sanctions.
Russia imported 368,000 metric tons of oil products by sea in August, 112,000 of them from South Korea, according to Kpler data analyzed by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) and cited by the Guardian. CREA's own August report gives 172,000 metric tons in total, including 18,000 from South Korea. Neither explains the gap.
Where the tankers said they were going
The Layla, a tanker under UK and EU sanctions, made two voyages from Ulsan to Vladivostok, carrying a total of 57,000 metric tons of diesel. It left South Korea on 19 July and 10 August. On the first trip, it told South Korean authorities it was bound for Vladivostok; on the second, it declared Niigata, Japan, but sailed to Vladivostok again.
The Astoria, a Russian-flagged tanker under UK, EU, and Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 metric tons of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August. It declared Japan as its destination but sailed to Vladivostok.
The Chongchon did not berth at a South Korean port. Instead, it took about 26,000 metric tons of fuel from the unsanctioned Celeste I at an anchorage off Yeosu in early August. It declared Singapore as its destination but headed to Vladivostok. The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to the Guardian's requests for comment.
Why Russia needs the fuel
Ukrainian drone strikes have severely disrupted Russia's refining capacity, the Guardian reported. In July, Ukraine's General Staff said the strikes had knocked out 42% of Russia's refining capacity, costing the industry billions of dollars.
Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years, and diesel output is down nearly 30% from a year earlier, the International Energy Agency said, according to the Guardian.
Russia has also restricted fuel exports to protect domestic supplies, extending its diesel export ban until the end of October; on 2 October, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow could consider partially lifting the ban if there was overproduction, according to the Moscow Times.
Responses to the shipments
Seoul's non-lethal aid has included helmets, body armor, and demining vehicles, and in 2023 it pledged $2.3 billion in support, mostly in loans.
Isaac Levi, an analyst at CREA, told the Guardian:
"It is shocking that EU-sanctioned tankers loaded fuel at South Korean ports and carried it to Russia. This undermines the sanctions regime and South Korea's support for Ukraine."
South Korea's Foreign Ministry did not address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said the government supports international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery. The ministry said it was strictly enforcing its export controls and had expanded them to cover 1,402 non-strategic items with high potential for diversion to military use. The UK Foreign Office did not answer the Guardian's questions about UK-sanctioned tankers using South Korean ports, saying only that it remains committed to monitoring its sanctions.
Ties between Kyiv and Seoul are also strained over Ukraine's disclosure of its transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul said should have remained private.

articles.title: Iran’s defense industry reaches new capacity as army chief warns enemies of ‘Historic Confusion’
articles.body:
Iran’s defense industry reaches new capacity as army chief warns enemies of ‘Historic Confusion’
TEHRAN — Iran’s indigenous defense industry has maintained uninterrupted production through the recent US-Israeli war and expanded its weapons production capacity to 2.5 times its pre-war level, senior Iranian military officials said, stressing that any renewed aggression would face a stronger response with more advanced weapons.
Army Commander Major General Amir Hatami said Iran’s adversaries were facing “historic confusion” in the face of the power and resilience of the Iranian nation.
Hatami made the remarks during a meeting with Mehrdad Akhlaqi, the nominee for Iran’s Minister of Defense and the current managing director of the Defense Industries Organization.
The Army chief commended the efforts of specialized, committed, and revolutionary personnel in Iran’s defense industry during the wars of aggression imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime, saying enemy attempts to disrupt the production chain for military equipment and weapons had failed.
He said defense-industry production lines “did not stop serving and working for a moment” even during the most critical circumstances of the aggression, enabling Iran’s Armed Forces to maintain their capabilities and preventing the enemy from achieving its objectives.
Hatami said the recent war demonstrated that Iran’s indigenous defense industry had become a strong and reliable support for the country’s combat forces and would continue to fulfill that role.
He added that, under the guidance of the Leader of the Islamic Revolution, Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei, and through the vigilant presence of the Iranian people and the efforts of the Armed Forces, “all the enemy’s calculations and objectives have been defeated.”
“The sworn enemies of the Islamic Republic are facing historic confusion in the face of the power of the great Iranian nation and engage in empty rhetoric every day,” Hatami said.
Akhlaqi, for his part, expressed hope that Iran’s Armed Forces would continue their achievements and secure the “final victory,” namely the expulsion of the United States from the region.
Iran’s weapons production capacity rises 2.5-fold
Separately, Defense Ministry spokesman Brigadier General Reza Talaei-Nik said Iran’s weapons production capacity has increased to 2.5 times its level before the war, stressing that any new aggression would be met with a more powerful response and more advanced weapons.
Speaking at a press conference on Tuesday, Talaei-Nik said enemy psychological operations and moves suggesting the possibility of renewed aggression would be met with a decisive response and heavier defeats for the adversary.
He described the removal of the United States from the region and the suppression of the Zionist regime’s acts of aggression as achievements of Iran’s defense during the recent US-Israeli war.
“The punishment of the American and Zionist murderers is the firm resolve of the Islamic Republic and will never be forgotten,” he said.
Talaei-Nik attributed the sharp rise in production capacity to the full mobilization of Iran’s defense-industrial capabilities, saying the country’s strategic depth in defense production had become an important component of national power and had strengthened Iran’s resilience in confronting its adversaries.
He said Iran’s production plans for offensive equipment were being continuously updated in accordance with developments in warfare and under the direction of the Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters and the General Staff of the Armed Forces, based on requirements identified by military commanders.
According to the Defense Ministry spokesman, Iran has the capacity to produce more than 1,000 weapons systems and military equipment, with some systems capable of being upgraded and manufactured in larger quantities in accordance with operational requirements.
“If the enemy makes a wrong calculation, it will definitely face more advanced weapons and a heavy response from the Armed Forces,” Talaei-Nik warned.
Iran, Russia and China deepen defense consultations
Talaei-Nik also pointed to the longstanding cooperation and convergence among Iran, Russia and China, saying active relations among the three countries have been supported by all sides.
He said defense-related exchanges of views with Russia and China were on Iran’s agenda, underlining Tehran’s continued engagement with the two countries in the defense field.

articles.title: Lithuania Moves to Lift Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Weapons on Its Territory
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Lithuania Moves to Lift Constitutional Ban on Nuclear Weapons on Its Territory
Lithuania’s parliament has backed a constitutional amendment that would remove the country’s ban on weapons of mass destruction, including nuclear weapons, being stationed on Lithuanian territory, LRT reported on October 6.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The proposed amendment would remove part of Article 137 of Lithuania’s Constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases from being located on the country’s territory. The proposal under consideration concerns the provision on weapons of mass destruction.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said removing the restriction would strengthen Lithuania’s resilience and deterrence capabilities while eliminating legal differences between Lithuania and other EU and NATO members.
Opposition Conservative leader Laurynas Kasčiūnas, who supported the amendment, said Lithuania’s existing restrictions prevent allied aircraft or ships carrying nuclear weapons from entering the country for deterrence purposes.
“With the current restriction, we cannot fully participate in NATO’s nuclear deterrence plans. Since nuclear deterrence is the queen of all deterrence, this decision is strategically important,” Kasčiūnas said.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas also supported the change, linking the initiative to the security environment created by Russia’s war against Ukraine and the presence of strategic weapons in Belarus and Russia’s Kaliningrad region.
“We are responding to Russia’s aggression. If Russia had not started the war in Ukraine, we probably would not be having the discussions that we are having today,” Kaunas said.
The debate over Lithuania’s constitutional restrictions also follows recent Russian nuclear threats involving Kaliningrad, the heavily militarized Russian exclave bordering Poland and Lithuania. On September 30, Reuters reported that Moscow had privately warned NATO it could resort to nuclear weapons if the alliance sought to isolate the region.
In a diplomatic note sent to NATO and reviewed by Reuters, Russia accused the alliance of pursuing a “dangerous and reckless course” that posed “high risks of the outbreak of a direct armed conflict.”
